title: The book with a family tree
hookLine: before a word on love, the book recites its family tree
carry: dharma, artha and kama: one life, three aims
tomorrow: a book on pleasure argues against pleasure. who wins?

lines: A BOOK THAT OPENS WITH ITS FAMILY TREE.
cards: The wedding hasn't started and an uncle already has the microphone. Before anyone dances, he walks the room through the family: whose son, whose grandson, which village, which great-grandmother opened the sweet shop.
A few people roll their eyes. Then they lean in, because the list says who belongs to whom. An old book well-known for something else entirely opens the same way.
Before a single word on love, the Kama Sutra stops and recites its family tree. And the name at the very top is a surprise.

teach.b: At the top is Prajapati, the creator. In the book's opening, he sets down one vast teaching on how people should live. Not three books.
Then the teaching is divided among three heirs. Manu takes the part on dharma, doing right. Brihaspati takes the part on artha, wealth and a living.
And Nandi, Shiva's attendant, takes the part on kama, pleasure and love. Later teachers keep shortening and splitting their shares, the text says, until the pieces are scattered.
Vatsyayana, the author, says he gathered them back into one small book. So notice what the family tree does. A book on desire doesn't introduce itself as a rebel or a secret.
It introduces itself as a sibling of the law books, with the same parent.

teach.h: THE PURUSHARTHAS: THE AIMS OF LIFE.
teach.b: Hindus call these the purusharthas, the aims of a human life, and in this telling kama was never outside dharma.
All three aims begin as one plan for one life, and split only because the plan grew too big for anyone to carry. That's why this path reads the ethics chapter and leaves the rest on the shelf.
The rest is a frank handbook for adults. The opening is an argument about how three aims fit together in one person, and its first move is to say: we're family.

how: Today the Kama Sutra is studied by students of Sanskrit and of Indian history, and some read its opening chapters on the three aims of life alongside the dharma texts and the Arthashastra.

games.q: what does “the kama sutra's ethics chapter” mean?
o: the opening that fits pleasure into one plan for a life
a list of vows for monks who give up all pleasure
a set of court rules for a king and his whole army

games.q: who takes which part of the one teaching? tap the pairs.
p: sets down the single, vast teaching

s: the Kama Sutra opens with a chapter on love
it opens with where its teaching came from, and how it fits beside dharma and wealth.
in the book's telling, dharma, artha and kama begin as one teaching
the creator sets it down whole; it's divided later.
Vatsyayana says he invented the whole subject himself
he says he gathered the scattered pieces of an older teaching into one small book.

games.q: your family's restaurant was split among three cousins long ago: one runs the kitchen, one the books, one the catering. you're writing its story for the menu. how would the Kama Sutra's opening tell it?
o: start with the one founder, then show how the shares split.
start with the cousin whose part is the most fun.
leave the split out; it makes the family look divided.
games.why: the book starts at the top, with Prajapati's one teaching, then shows it divided among Manu, Brihaspati and Nandi. the split is part of the family story, not a scandal.

practice: Take a scrap of paper and write three short lines: one thing you do because it's right, one thing you do for a living or for school, and one thing you simply enjoy.
Above them, draw a single line joining all three, like a family tree with one parent. Then sit with the page, ranking none of them.

wordCard.voice: The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: the book's opening, where pleasure, right living and wealth come down from one teaching.

orig.note: Sanskrit kamasutra, the name of Vatsyayana's book.

carryVoice: Keep this one: dharma, artha and kama, one life with three aims, all from one parent. Day fifteen ninety-seven, done.
